description.summary: Milvus is an open-source cloud-native vector database that combines distributed dense and sparse vector retrieval, scalar filtering, BM25 full-text retrieval, and configurable hybrid reranking.
description.description: Milvus separates compute, storage, streaming, and coordination roles to support horizontally scalable vector retrieval. It provides exact, graph-based, inverted-file, quantized, GPU, sparse, and disk-oriented index families; standard and iterative metadata filtering; dense-sparse hybrid retrieval with weighted or reciprocal-rank reranking; configurable consistency levels; resource groups, replicas, and several multi-tenancy strategies. This record distinguishes documented capabilities from workload-, topology-, and deployment-dependent performance.

indexingConsiderations: Choose FLAT, HNSW, IVF, quantized, GPU, sparse, or DiskANN indexes only after measuring recall, latency, build time, memory, storage, and top-k behavior on representative data.
Use DiskANN when most vector data must remain on SSD and available memory cannot hold an in-memory graph, while accounting for storage latency and IOPS.
Create scalar indexes for fields used by production filters and assess their ingestion, storage, and compaction costs.
Plan collection shards, replicas, resource groups, object storage, WAL infrastructure, and query-node capacity before large-scale ingestion.
retrievalConsiderations: Evaluate dense-only, BM25-only, sparse-only, and hybrid retrieval on the same relevance set before choosing a ranker and its weights.
Compare standard pre-filtering with iterative filtering when expressions are complex or highly selective.
Treat each vector field and sparse representation as a separate retrieval channel with explicit metrics, indexes, candidate limits, and evaluation criteria.
Select strong, bounded, session, or eventual consistency according to data-visibility requirements and acceptable search latency.

limitations: Index families have workload-specific tradeoffs among recall, latency, build time, memory, storage, I/O, and operational cost.
DiskANN and memory-mapped configurations depend on SSD latency, throughput, page-cache behavior, and storage contention.
Complex scalar expressions can make standard pre-filtering expensive, while iterative filtering can perform additional vector-search work before collecting enough matches.
Dense-sparse fusion and reranker weights are relevance choices, not universally optimal defaults.
Bounded, session, and eventual consistency can expose data-visibility lags compared with strong consistency.
Distributed Milvus requires coordinated operation of metadata, WAL, object storage, compute nodes, compaction, replicas, and resource groups.
Multi-tenancy isolation and RBAC capabilities differ across database, collection, partition, and partition-key strategies.
Milvus does not provide general multi-record ACID transactions comparable to a relational database.
usageGuidance: Record the Milvus server and SDK versions because index, query, filter, text-search, and operational behavior changes across releases.
Use a representative relevance and load test before changing index families, filter modes, rankers, quantization, mmap, or consistency settings.
Use resource groups and replicas to isolate query workloads, but coordinate them with external cluster scaling and capacity planning.
Choose the multi-tenancy level from the required isolation, schema flexibility, tenant count, RBAC scope, and cross-tenant query requirements.
Test backup and restoration procedures and monitor WAL health, object storage, indexing queues, compaction, shard distribution, query latency, recall, and replica availability.

references.title: Milvus Documentation: Hybrid Search and BM25

claims.statement: Milvus supports exact, HNSW, IVF, quantized, sparse, GPU, and disk-oriented vector index families, including DiskANN for datasets that exceed available RAM.
claims.rationale: The official index catalog lists FLAT, IVF, HNSW, quantized, GPU, sparse, and disk-based choices, while the DiskANN documentation describes a disk-resident Vamana graph with in-memory PQ data.

claims.statement: Milvus supports metadata pre-filtering before ANN search and an iterative filtering mode for complex expressions that would make standard filtering expensive.

qualifiers.name: configurationScope
qualifiers.value: Filter efficiency depends on scalar indexes, expression complexity, selectivity, and vector index behavior

claims.rationale: The filtered-search documentation distinguishes standard metadata filtering before ANN from iterative vector retrieval followed by per-candidate filtering.

claims.statement: Milvus stores dense and sparse vector fields in one collection, provides a built-in BM25 sparse pipeline, and combines retrieval channels with weighted or reciprocal-rank reranking.

qualifiers.name: relevanceScope
qualifiers.value: Fusion methods and weights require evaluation on a representative relevance set

claims.rationale: Official hybrid-search examples use dense and sparse fields with BM25, WeightedRanker, and reciprocal-rank fusion.

claims.statement: Milvus uses a distributed storage-compute architecture with independently scalable worker roles, shared object storage, WAL durability, replicas, and query-node resource groups.

qualifiers.name: deploymentScope
qualifiers.value: Distributed self-hosted deployments require external orchestration and coordinated operation of metadata, WAL, object storage, and worker nodes

claims.rationale: The architecture documentation describes disaggregated access, coordination, streaming, query, data, and storage layers; resource groups isolate QueryNodes and coordinate collection replicas.

claims.statement: Milvus offers strong, bounded-staleness, session, and eventual consistency and supports multi-tenancy at database, collection, partition, and partition-key levels.

qualifiers.name: isolationScope
qualifiers.value: Isolation, tenant scale, schema flexibility, RBAC, and cross-tenant query behavior differ by multi-tenancy strategy

claims.rationale: The consistency documentation defines four selectable data-visibility levels, while the multi-tenancy guide compares four isolation levels and their operational tradeoffs.

evidence.summary: Official Milvus sources enumerate multiple CPU, GPU, sparse, quantized, graph, inverted-file, exact, and disk-oriented indexes.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can represent Milvus as a broad index platform with exact, in-memory ANN, compressed, sparse, GPU, and DiskANN options.

sourceFragments.locator: Supported vector index table and index selection guidance
DiskANN overview, Vamana graph, product quantization, and disk search process

limitations: Project documentation establishes supported features but is not an independent performance benchmark.
Index results depend on vectors, dimensions, hardware, data size, filters, top-k, build parameters, and search parameters.

evidence.summary: The filtered-search documentation describes standard filtering before ANN and iterative filtering during candidate collection.
evidence.interpretation: Milvus supports pre-filtered retrieval and an alternative iterative path rather than relying only on post-filtering a fixed result set.

sourceFragments.locator: Standard filtering and iterative filtering sections

limitations: Scalar indexes add storage, ingestion, and compaction cost.
Iterative filtering can examine additional candidates and may change latency predictability.

evidence.summary: Milvus hybrid-search documentation combines dense and sparse fields, built-in BM25 retrieval, and weighted or RRF reranking.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark built-in sparse lexical retrieval, dense-sparse hybrid search, weighted fusion, and reciprocal-rank fusion.

sourceFragments.locator: Dense, sparse, and hybrid retrieval example with WeightedRanker and reciprocal-rank fusion

limitations: No ranker or weighting scheme is universally best across relevance objectives.
Candidate limits and per-channel score distributions can materially affect fused rankings.

evidence.summary: Milvus documents disaggregated compute and storage layers, WAL and object-storage persistence, worker specialization, replicas, and QueryNode resource groups.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark high horizontal scaling and workload isolation while retaining the operational complexity of a distributed system.

sourceFragments.locator: Architecture layers, worker roles, object storage, WAL, and search data flow
Resource-group isolation, replicas, QueryNode transfer, and scaling guidance

limitations: Self-hosted deployments require external orchestration and capacity management.
Scaling, rebalancing, compaction, storage, and replica operations can interact under load.

evidence.summary: Milvus documents four consistency levels and four multi-tenancy strategies with different isolation and scalability properties.
evidence.interpretation: The RKM profile can mark configurable consistency and high multi-tenancy capability without treating all tenant models as equivalent.

sourceFragments.locator: Strong, bounded staleness, session, eventual, and GuaranteeTs sections
Database, collection, partition, and partition-key multi-tenancy comparison

limitations: Weaker consistency levels trade immediate visibility for lower latency or higher availability.
Partition and partition-key tenant models provide different RBAC and physical-isolation guarantees than database or collection models.
